How graph theory is applied

The map is a graph: each 0.1° cell is a node and each pair of side-by-side cells is an edge, 21,600 nodes and 42,900 edges. Past earthquakes are a signal on the nodes. Diffusion spreads that signal along the edges, and the forecast is the result.

Click any cell on the map above. Line thickness is the squared edge weight w². Thick edges lie along the local trend direction, so information flows freely along trends and weakly across them.

Select a cell.

Row i of (I + tL)x = ρ. L is the weighted graph Laplacian: each row sums to zero, so total count is conserved, and it is symmetric and positive semi-definite, so the system has one positive solution. Weights lie between 0 and 1, so the largest eigenvalue of L is at most 8 and conjugate gradients converge fast.

Read before presenting

What this replay shows

One forecast map per model, issued on 1 January 2026 and never refitted. Each earthquake of magnitude 3.0 or more from 1 January to 27 August 2026 (3,212 events, of which 417 are mainshocks that start a cluster) is placed on that map. A hit means the epicentre lies in a cell ranked in the top share of the map by forecast probability. Information gain measures how much more probability the model put on the observed cell than a uniform map would, in bits.

What it does not show

The model forecasts where, not when and not how large. Hits inside a flagged area are far above chance, but most of that skill comes from earthquakes recurring in already active zones. The test is pseudo-prospective, not blind, because 2026 had been examined in an earlier analysis with a different catalog. The settings were chosen on 2025 only, and the forecast was not changed after scoring began.

How the models compare in the study

The hybrid (equal mix of the sheaf model, the adaptive kernel and the fitted ETAS model) has the highest pooled information gain, 1.726 bits, and is clearly better than the sheaf model alone (+0.18 bits, adjusted p = 0.002). It is statistically tied with the best single models on pooled information gain, and the fitted ETAS model scores higher on mainshocks and per cluster. The fault layer did not add measurable skill. Use the table above to show these differences openly.

Place names, probabilities and area selection

Each cell is named with the nearest PHIVOLCS reference town and the distance and direction from it, in the same wording as the bulletin. The reference towns come from the bulletin itself: every “km, direction, town” entry was converted back to the town’s position, and the median over many events was used. Forecast probability is the cell’s share of the whole forecast. A selected box adds up the cells inside it and compares the sum with the share of earthquakes that actually fell there.

How to verify a forecast with new earthquakes

Pick the forecast, upload the PHIVOLCS list for the period after it was made, and read the share of earthquakes that fell inside the flagged area. The forecast issued on 28 Aug 2026 uses the study catalog to 27 Aug 2026 and the study’s fault-free sheaf model, so earthquakes from 28 Aug onward are new to it. The 1 Jan 2026 forecasts are never refitted, so they are checked on events from 1 Jan onward. Mainshocks are found in the browser with Gardner–Knopoff windows. A hit rate above the chance level (the flagged share) shows skill; the size of the gap, not the hit rate alone, is what matters.

About the forecast built from your upload

The browser runs the fault-free sheaf model (A) with the study settings and compares it with smoothed seismicity. Its output matches the study's Python code to better than one part in ten million. It does not run the fitted ETAS model, the adaptive kernel, the hybrid or the fault layer, and it does not decluster, so hit rates count aftershocks. On short windows the numbers are noisy: for the 1 to 27 August 2026 sample, smoothed seismicity scores slightly higher than the sheaf model, which agrees with the study's finding that the sheaf model does not beat the best simple baselines.

Data: PHIVOLCS earthquake bulletin, 2019 to 27 August 2026. Coastline: Natural Earth via world-atlas. Numbers in this page are computed in the browser from the saved forecast maps and match the study's result files.
